What is being compressed?

Stored scalars
Storage vs. originalCounting scalars, not bytes
Relative Frobenius errorBefore pixel clipping

A grayscale image of height m and width n is represented by a matrix A of size m × n. Each entry aij records the brightness of the pixel in row i and column j, on a scale from 0 (black) to 255 (white).

Let r=rank(A). The singular value decomposition (SVD) expresses A as a sum of r rank-one matrices:

A=∑i=1rσiuiviT

Here the singular values are ordered so that

σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σr>0

The vectors ui∈ℝm and vi∈ℝn are the corresponding left and right singular vectors, respectively, and each family is orthonormal.

To compress the image, choose an integer 0≤k≤r and retain only the first k terms of the SVD. This gives the rank-at-most-k approximation

Ak=∑i=1kσiuiviT

The original matrix stores mn entries. The truncated factors store mk entries in U, k singular values, and nk entries in V: k(m+n+1) scalars.

The Eckart–Young theorem guarantees that Ak minimizes the Frobenius error among matrices of rank at most k.

‖A−Ak‖F=∑i=k+1rσi2

The relative Frobenius error is defined as

‖A−Ak‖F‖A‖F

Original pixel brightness is encoded by integers from 0 (black) to 255 (white). Truncated SVD can produce entries outside this interval. Displayed pixels are rounded and clipped to [0,255], so the displayed matrix need not have rank at most k. The error uses the mathematical approximation before clipping or rounding. This demo counts stored scalars rather than actual encoded file size.

Image sources: Cameraman and Cat (Chelsea) are from the scikit-image sample collection. The remaining images are generated synthetically.
